title: What Is the Difference Between a Pastor and a Therapist?
subtitle: On soul care, the difference between a pastor and a therapist, and the wisdom to know when to refer

sections.title: The Chair Across From You
sections.body:
Someone closes your office door and sits down, and the air changes. They have rehearsed the first sentence in the car. They are about to tell you something they have told no one, and they are watching your face to see whether they were right to risk it.

This is holy ground, and it is dangerous ground, and most of us were never trained for either.

What they need first is not your answer. It is your attention. So give it whole. Put the phone in a drawer. Stop composing your reply while they are still speaking, because they can see you doing it and it tells them you are not safe. The single most useful thing you will do in that hour is listen long enough that the real thing surfaces, and the real thing almost never comes out in the first ten minutes. The presenting problem is the doorway. It is not the room. I have rushed to fix the doorway a hundred times and missed the room entirely. I wanted to be the man with the answer. The man with the answer is often the man who stopped listening.

sections.title: Soul Care Is Not Therapy
sections.body:
You are a pastor. You are not a psychologist, and the day you forget the difference is the day you become dangerous to the people who trust you most.

The pastor tends the soul before God. The therapist treats the mind with clinical training you do not have.

These overlap, and they are not the same, and pretending otherwise has wrecked people. You can sit with a grieving widow and point her to the God who keeps her tears in a bottle. You cannot diagnose her depression, you cannot manage her medication, and you cannot treat the trauma that may be underneath her grief. That is not your office and it was never meant to be. There is a strain of teaching that says every problem is a sin problem and every answer is in the text, and that teaching has told clinically depressed people to repent of an illness and sent suicidal people home with a verse and a handshake. I have watched that done. It is not faithfulness. It is malpractice wearing a Bible. The Scriptures are sufficient for everything they claim to be sufficient for. They do not claim to be a substitute for the doctor who set your broken arm, and a broken brain is no different from a broken arm except that we have been slower to believe it is real.

sections.title: When to Refer, and How
sections.body:
Know the signs that the conversation has moved past your door, and know them cold, because lives depend on you knowing them.

Refer when you hear a plan to die. Refer when you hear of harm to a child. Refer when the darkness will not lift, when the eating has stopped or will not stop, when the drinking runs the house, when you hear voices described that no one else can hear, when the person cannot function at the basic level of getting out of bed for weeks. These are not weak faith. These are conditions that need a clinician, and your job is to get them to one without making them feel abandoned by God or by you.

Referral is not failure. Referral is love that knows its own limits.

So build the bridge before you need it. Keep a short list of licensed counselors you trust, ideally some who share the faith and some who simply do their work well. Know the number for the crisis line and keep it where you can find it in a panic, because the call will come when you are not ready. When you refer, do not hand someone off like a package. Say I am still your pastor and I am still here, and this person can help you in a way I am not trained to. Then follow up. Walk them to the door of the help they need and keep walking with them on the other side of it. A referral done in love says you matter too much for me to be the only one in this with you.

sections.title: The Care Only You Can Give
sections.body:
Now hear the other half, because in our rush to refer we can forget there is real work that is ours alone, work no therapist is licensed to do.

The counselor cannot pronounce forgiveness. You can. The counselor cannot bring the body and blood to the table. You can.

When a man tells you the sin that has been eating him alive for thirty years, you get to do the thing the angels long to witness. You get to tell him, on the authority of the cross, that in Christ it is forgiven, that the blood covers exactly this, that he can walk out from under a weight he has carried since before his children were born. No clinician can say that sentence. It is not in their scope. It is the center of yours. You can pray with people. You can read the Word over their fear. You can remind a saint who has forgotten that they belong to God and that nothing in death or life can change it. This is soul care, and it is not a lesser thing than therapy. It is a different thing, and a holy one, and it is the thing you were ordained for.

sections.title: What This Work Costs You
sections.body:
You will absorb things. Secrets that do not leave when the person does. Stories you cannot tell anyone, that sit in you and accumulate, that wake you at three in the morning years later.

This work has weight, and the weight does not vanish because you are the pastor. It collects.

So you need your own people. A spiritual director, a counselor of your own, a circle of fellow pastors where you can lay down what you are not permitted to carry alone. Protect confidence ferociously, and at the same time refuse to become the lonely sin-eater of the whole congregation, because that road ends in burnout, in cynicism, or in moral collapse, and I have seen all three. Keep the Sabbath you preach to others. Stay under the Word as a hearer and not only a handler of it. The shepherd who never lies down in green pastures will not be able to lead anyone there. You cannot pour from a soul you never let God fill, and the people across from you deserve a pastor who is still being pastored by someone himself.
